L31: Cultural and artistic life in the city is explored through the stories of the scribe, the printer and the artist, the intricate and international network of diplomatic and mercantile exchanges along the trading routes is revealed through stories from the merchant, the diplomat and the fortune-teller and the enduring legacy of Dunhuang as a site of pilgrimage and worship is illustrated through the Buddhist nun and the lay Buddhist.
L32: This year marks the 30th anniversary of the cite17†International Dunhuang Programme†idp.bl.uk , a global collaboration committed to digitising, preserving and increasing access to the manuscripts from the Eastern Silk Roads, and the exhibition brings together documents and objects from Dunhuang, many for the very first time.
L33: ## Highlights include:
L34:   * The Diamond Sutra (868 AD), the world’s earliest complete printed book with a date, and one of the most influential Mahayana sutras in East Asia.
L35:   * The Dunhuang star chart (649-700), the earliest known manuscript atlas of the night sky from any civilisation
L36:   * A rubbing of the Stele of Sulaiman, a carved stone slab that was erected in 1348 at the Mogao Caves, on display for the first time
L37:   * A copy of the Diamond Sutra written in the scribe’s own blood, considered an act of powerful sincerity when copying Buddhist scriptures, on display for the first time.
L38:   * The Old Tibetan Annals (641-761), the earliest surviving historical document in Tibetan
L39:   * A manuscript fragment dating from the 9th century about the prophet Zoroaster or Zarathusra, nearly 400 years older than any other surviving Zoroastrian scripture.
L40:   * The longest surviving manuscript text in the Old Turkic script, a Turkic omen text known as the Irk Bitig or Book of Omens (930 or 942)
L41:   * A paper stencil (800-1000) believed to create the thousand-Buddha motif featured on the ceilings of many Mogao Caves
L42:   * One of the most important and complete manuscripts among the Old Uyghur Manichaean texts, the Xuastuanift, a confessional book of Manichaean Uyghurs, on display for the first time
L43:   * A recently conserved 9th-10th century painting depicting the 11-headed manifestation of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, on display for the first time.
L44: A Silk Road Oasis: Life in Ancient Dunhuang also features an immersive soundscape recreating the sounds of the ancient Silk Road based on recordings from the British Library’s sound archive and the China Database for Traditional Music, coordinated by Dr. Xiaoshi Wei.
L45: The soundscape blends contemporary material from artists across historic Silk Road nations, such as Iran and Kazakhstan, and includes newly commissioned works by Tibetan folk artist Ngawang Lodup, Uyghur virtuoso Shorhet Nur and Chinese musician Wu Fei.
L46: Mélodie Doumy, Lead Curator, Chinese Collections (Stein and Hoernle) and International Dunhuang Programme manager at the British Library, said: 'We are incredibly excited to provide a glimpse into the lives of the ordinary people who were the heart and soul of the Dunhuang oasis, making it such a fascinating melting-pot of languages, cultures and religions.

L87: #### Stencil for ‘Thousand Buddha’ motif
L88: This pounce or stencil was one of nine from the Dunhuang cache of manuscripts. These designs, with holes punctured at intervals along thick, black lines, were used to produce the repetitive ‘Thousand Buddha’ designs on cave ceilings painted in the 9th and 10th centuries. The upper sections of cave-shrines were difficult to reach and the design demanded the execution of identical figures. In order to produce these images, one would place the pounce against the wall and apply powder over its surface.
L90: Examples of the ‘Thousand Buddha’ motif can be found in many of the Mogao caves in Dunhuang. Repetition of the Buddha’s image was believed to be one way of spreading his word and generating karmic merit. It also relates to a core Mahayana teaching, that every sentient being has the potential to achieve Buddhahood.

L152: This is a photograph of the Mogao Caves, a complex of nearly 500 monastic caves in Dunhuang, Gansu Province. Sir Marc Aurel Stein, a Hungarian-born British archaeologist, took the photograph in 1914 during his third expedition to the Mogao site.
L153: The Mogao Caves, meaning ‘peerless caves’, were carved directly into cliff faces by Buddhist monks and were used as quiet spaces for worship and meditation. Hundreds of caves were excavated between the 4th and 14th centuries CE. Dunhuang, an oases city at the intersection of the ancient Silk Roads, became a pilgrimage spot and a hub of Buddhist practice.
L154: Today, the caves contain some of the best surviving examples of ancient Buddhist art, including wall murals, portable paintings, sculptures carved directly into the walls, textiles, and various devotional objects. One cave, known as Cave 17, was filled with manuscripts and sealed around 1000 CE. Its rediscovery in 1900 revealed an unrivalled source for knowledge of official and religious life in Dunhuang.

L1008: This bilingual scroll contains a report written by a prominent Khotanese diplomat, known in Chinese as Zhang Jinshan and in Khotanese as Ca Kima-Sana. He is mentioned in several documents from Dunhuang.
L1009: At the top of the manuscript, Ca Kima-Sana writes of his visit to the Mogao Caves. He recalls lighting lanterns, burning incense and praying to the Buddha. The section in inscribed in Chinese, but written from left to right, which is an unconventional choice perhaps influenced by the direction of Khotanese script.
L1010: Below this text, a section in Khotanese recounts how he lead a delegation of 115 people from Khotan to Dunhuang in a mission to secure the hand of a Chinese princess for his king. This is an example of the many marriage alliances binding the ruling families of Khotan and Dunhuang across several generations.

L1094: The Old Tibetan Annals are the earliest surviving Tibetan history records. The text gives a year-by-year account of the Tibetan imperial court during its initial expansion into nearby territories. Before the scroll’s discovery in Cave 17, no contemporary accounts from this period were known. It  has enabled historians to verify events mentioned in later historical sources.
L1095: Together with the Old cite164†Tibetan Chronicle , the Old Tibetan Annals provide an unprecedented account of Tibetan history and  constitute one of the earliest examples of Old Tibetan script. ‘Old Tibetan’ or ‘Classical Tibetan’ was the first form of Tibetan script, devised by Thonmi Sambhota at the beginning of the Tibetan Empire. It was based on the oral Tibetan language and Indian Sanskrit script.
L1096: The text survives in two manuscripts originally from the same scroll, now held in two separate collections. One half, known as the cite165†‘Civil’ version , covers the years 650 to 748 CE and is at the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The other half, known as the ‘Military’ version, covers the years 743 to 765 CE and lives at the British Library.

L1109: This Chinese copy of the Diamond Sutra, complete with an ornate illustrated ‘frontispiece’, is the world’s earliest dated, printed book. It was one of the most significant ancient Buddhist items discovered in Mogao Cave 17, or ‘the Library Cave’ near Dunhuang.
L1110: The Diamond Sutra was first translated from Sanskrit into Chinese around 400 CE. As noted in the colophon (a note at the end of the scroll), the production of this copy was sponsored by Wang Jie on 11 May 868. The text was woodblock printed onto seven sheets of yellow-dyed paper, joined together to form a 5-metre long horizontal  scroll.
L1111: The Diamond Sutra is one of the most important sutras in Mahayana Buddhism. In Sanskrit, it is known as Vajracchedikasutra, which roughly translates to ‘The Diamond that Cuts through Illusion’. This refers to the Buddhist concept of Prajna – the wisdom that, like an indestructible diamond, cuts through ignorance and reveals the nature of reality.
L1112: The text itself takes the form of a conversation between the Buddha and his disciple Subhuti, who discuss the Buddhist belief that the material world is an illusion.

L1125: This 9th century silk banner painting is one of the best-preserved examples from Dunhuang, with its headpiece, weighting board and streamers still intact.
L1126: The banner has distinctive details such as the moss-green side streamers hanging over the main painting, and the bottom streamers decorated with scrolling foliage. Most striking, however, is the bodhisattva figure, unconventionally depicted from the back with his head turned in a sideways glance. He stands on a lotus flower and holds a glass beaker.
L1127: The silk is thin enough that the painting can be seen from both sides. This would have been a practical design feature for an item intended to be carried on a staff in procession, or attached to a stupa.

L151: Depicted in this painting is a bodhisattva Bodhisattva In Theravada Buddhism, the name for a person on the path to enlightenment, often used for the previous lives of the Buddha. In Mahayana Buddhism, a fully enlightened being who remains in samsara through compassion for others. Some bodhisattvas such as Avalokitesvara are the object of prayers and devotional rituals. cite8†Explore the Glossary , identified by the characters Yinlupu, which mean ‘Bodhisattva guide of souls’.
L152: Thought to be Avalokitesvara, the bodhisattva leads the soul of a woman to the Pure Land, this theme appears to have been popular in the 9th to 10th centuries, with several examples found at Dunhuang.
L153: As is common in these compositions, the bodhisattva takes up most of the space in the painting. In one hand, he holds a lotus flower with a banner attached to its stem. In the other, he burns incense in a hand-censer. Following closely behind him is a small female donor figure. Both are travelling on the same cloud, and the smoke from the censer leads up to the paradise of the Pure Land, represented by a Chinese-style building in the upper left corner.
L154: The figures are rendered in a rich colour palette of deep red, pale green and yellow gold, with a touch of gold-leaf detailing.

L167: Monk Daozhen was abbot of the Sanjie Temple in 10th-century Dunhuang. He wrote this manuscript, found in Cave 17, which sets out his intention to restore the library at his monastery:
L168: > On [the 29th of July, 9341, the disciple of Sanjie monastery, the monk Daozhen, having seen that among the contents of the storehouse of his temple the sets of scriptures and commentaries were incomplete, there upon bowed his forehead to the ground and, with devout sincerity, took an oath and made a prayer: “I will go carefully through the cartons and storehouses of all the families, seeking after sold and decayed scriptural texts.
L169: I will gather them in the monastery, repair and patch them from beginning to end, and pass them down the ages. Their light will beautify the gate of mystery for ten thousand generations and one thousand autumns.
